doc.title: Bill Crow interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995

title: Trumpet, baritone horn and tuba in school
summary: Under teacher Al Benest he starts trumpet in fourth grade, is moved to baritone horn, and is later offered tuba at the University of Washington.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: So when did the bass come into the picture here?

Well it’s funny. I was a brass player all the time I was a kid. I wanted to be, my mother started me on piano and I hit a wall about the John M. Williams second book I think. I couldn’t get both hands to pay attention to what they were doing. But in the fourth grade a wonderful man came to our school, Al Benest was his name, and took over the whole music system from high school to grade school. He saw that he didn’t have much to work with because the previous person had been kind of perfunctory and his whole band was graduating that year and nothing was coming up. So I was in the fourth grade, he came down and passed out sheets of paper and said who wants to play what instrument, I’ll talk to your folks. So I knew what a trumpet was and I thought that was probably a nice instrument. So I wrote down trumpet. And he came and talked to my mom and dad and they agreed that they would get me one. Now they were poor as church mice at the time but there was a trumpet in the Sears Roebuck catalogue for $9.95 with case, and that’s what they got me. Now I had to wait a week to get it, the shipping of it was kind of slow. So I went to the band rehearsals every morning with the other kids and I’d sit there and watch them fingering, and then when I finally got my horn I was playing more watching their fingerings. But I had great ears, and I would learn the music within a day or two, if we played it twice I had it. So I didn’t get to be a good reader right away, I was a good © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

listener and a kind of a sad reader. But by the time I was in the sixth grade I was disappointed that I couldn’t play the melodies. I couldn’t get enough lip to play the high notes so they wouldn’t put me on first. And I complained to the teacher, and he said, “Well let me see your teeth,” you know, and he says, “you may never really get a good trumpet embouchure with those front teeth.” I got a pair of front teeth that stick out a little bit. But he said, “The school owns a baritone horn. It has a bigger mouthpiece, the music reads just the same as the trumpet, and it has all the good parts” he tells me. Which is true — when they transcribe from the orchestra to the concert band, they take all the cello parts and give them to the baritone horn. And the clincher was he told me he had played that instrument at one time. I knew he was a trombone player. So and I was crazy about him so I said, “All right, I’ll try it.” By this time I think my dad had gotten me a $40 trumpet that was made out of silver instead of brass, hoping that that would help me out. It didn’t, so when I got this school horn, he took the horn back and got his money back and I was out of the trumpet business. Well it turned out that the baritone horn was a beautiful instrument. I loved it and I learned to play it well, and by the time I was in high school I got an after school job and bought a horn of my own that was really a good sounding instrument. And I would win solo contests and you know, I was considered an exceptional baritone horn player. When I got into college, I went to the University of Washington for a little while before I went in the army. And they had all of the baritone chairs were full. I couldn’t be a baritone horn player there. I was crushed. But they offered me an E flat tuba, which I tried, sousaphone—
Getting lower and lower as you go on.
